title: Hospital pharmacy: substitution errors during drug shortages, two empty searches confirmed, privacy decision pending
notes: Demanding path with nothing retrieved. The need names a retrospective review (routing explicit). The first recorded fixture search returns HTTP 200 with zero records. A scan reply (shape discovery, certainty keys omitted) offers four model leads, one with no year, no method score and no grade: they are stored as unverified leads with unknowns kept unknown, and the stage stays incomplete, shown as leads only (G1 to G4). A second, broader search is also empty. The investigator then confirms on screen that the search was run and returned nothing; only this completes the stage, recorded as an investigator action tied to the query (D20; A3.2 part 1 and D26), and certainty stays unassessed ('not assessed') because nothing was inspected. With no appraisal there are no ledger claims, so the design decision is a claimless 'narrow' decision (no text contradicted, acceptable as a selection) whose privacy gate stays unknown to the end: the action stays blocked (G7; A2 item 9). A second protocol reply removes the theoretical framework with an explicit null: a model-owned field is cleared to '' with issue 'cleared' (the investigator's constraints are never the target, G11). No record is retrieved, so no record ids exist in this scenario. Catches: certainty or completion over empty searches, a model field that completes the stage, invented defaults for unknown lead values, a gate met without evidence, and an explicit null that fails to clear a model-owned field.

inputs.need:
I manage the medication safety program in the pharmacy department of Ellery Park Hospital, a 600-bed teaching hospital. Between March 2024 and October 2025 we had three shortages that forced us to substitute products: premixed potassium chloride bags were replaced by a different concentration, an intravenous antibiotic came in a different vial size that needed a new dilution, and a paediatric oral solution was replaced by a product with a different concentration. Each time we sent out alerts and changed the electronic prescribing entries, but staff told us about near misses, and I suspect some errors reached patients.

I want to do a retrospective review of our incident reports and the pharmacy intervention log to estimate how often the substitutions were followed by medication errors, what kinds of errors happened (wrong dose, wrong dilution, wrong rate, wrong product selected), where in the medication process they occurred, and whether the rate differed between the three shortages. Incident reports in our system are not flagged as shortage-related, so we will have to search the free text and match dates and products. The pharmacy intervention log lists every prescription a pharmacist changed, which may catch errors that were never reported as incidents.

I would also like to know what other hospitals have found, and whether there is a standard way to define a shortage-related error. The results are meant to shape how we manage the next shortage, not to blame staff. The hospital privacy office has not yet told us whether incident reports can be used for research without asking patients for consent.
inputs.constraints: Existing incident reports and the pharmacy intervention log only; chart review limited to 150 cases. One pharmacy resident for 100 hours between November 2026 and April 2027. Results reported by shortage episode, never naming staff or wards.
localFacts: Three shortage episodes required product substitution between 2024-03-01 and 2025-10-31: premixed potassium chloride bags, an intravenous antibiotic vial size, and a paediatric oral solution concentration.
The incident reporting system logged 1,204 medication incidents between 2024-03-01 and 2025-10-31; none is flagged as shortage-related.
The hospital privacy office has not decided whether incident reports can be used for research without patient consent.

response.subtitle: Three shortage episodes, 2024 to 2025, Ellery Park Hospital
response.statement: Three drug shortages between March 2024 and October 2025 forced product substitutions with different concentrations or vial sizes. Staff reported near misses, but shortage-related incidents are not flagged and nobody knows how often substitutions were followed by errors, of what kind, where in the medication process, or whether some substitutions were riskier than others.
response.whoAffected: Inpatients, including children, receiving the substituted products; nurses, prescribers and pharmacists who handle substitutions; the medication safety program.
response.whatHurts: Concentration and dilution changes can lead to wrong doses or rates, including with high-alert medicines such as intravenous potassium.
response.currentPractice: Alerts and electronic prescribing changes at each substitution; no review of what happened afterwards.
response.whyNow: Shortages recur and the next substitution plan should be informed by what went wrong in the last three.
response.constraints: Existing incident reports and the pharmacy intervention log only; chart review limited to 150 cases. One pharmacy resident for 100 hours between November 2026 and April 2027. Results reported by shortage episode, never naming staff or wards.
response.patientCenteredGoal: Patients receive the right dose at the right rate when a product has to be substituted.
response.summary: Problem framed as a retrospective review of substitution-related errors in three shortage episodes.

response.synthesis: The recorded search returned nothing. From general knowledge, four leads may be worth checking: a national survey of pharmacists on shortage-related errors, a paediatric study of concentration changes, a consensus definition, and a case series on potassium substitutions. None has been retrieved or read.

contexts: incident reports not flagged for shortages
response.reading: A substitution changes the product that prescribers, pharmacists and nurses see, and errors can enter at prescribing, preparation or administration. Incident reports capture what staff chose to report; the intervention log captures what pharmacists intercepted; neither alone gives the error rate. No external evidence was retrieved, so the local data must carry the analysis.

response.designSummary: Descriptive rates per 1,000 doses by episode, with the pre-episode rate for the original product as a baseline.
response.sampleSize: All doses and reports in the defined periods are included, so there is no sampling. With perhaps 2,000 to 10,000 doses per episode and error rates of a few per 1,000, each rate will have a wide interval; the analysis is descriptive and compares episodes cautiously.
response.primaryAnalysis: Rate per 1,000 doses with exact Poisson 95 percent confidence intervals for each episode and its baseline period; rate ratio of episode to baseline per product.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Error type and stage by episode; proportion reaching the patient.
response.missingData: Incident reports without a product name are reviewed by date and ward; unresolvable reports are counted and reported.
response.multiplicity: Three episodes described; no formal testing between them.
response.software: R for rates and exact intervals.
overfittingGuards: No modelling beyond rates and rate ratios
response.summary: Descriptive rates with exact intervals and a pre-episode baseline.

response.risks: Privacy of patients named in incident reports; blame of staff if results identify individuals or wards.
response.consent: Research use without individual consent depends on the privacy office's decision; if refused, the work proceeds only as internal quality review under existing safety policy, without publication.
response.data: Extraction into a de-identified dataset on the pharmacy's restricted drive; no staff or ward names; results by episode only.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: children (the paediatric oral solution) and patients with limited English, who may be less able to question an unfamiliar product, are considered; the paediatric episode is reported separately.
response.partnerships: Medication safety committee, nursing practice leads, paediatric pharmacy team.

response.limitations: Under-reporting; one hospital; no external comparison.

response.title: Medication errors after product substitution in three drug shortages at a teaching hospital: a retrospective review
response.abstract: Objective: to estimate substitution-related medication error rates per 1,000 doses dispensed in three shortage episodes, with pre-episode baselines for the original products. Design: retrospective review of incident reports and the pharmacy intervention log. Results will be reported if research use of incident reports is approved.
response.introduction: Shortages force substitutions that change concentrations, vial sizes and preparation steps. Local error rates during substitutions are rarely measured, and incident reports are not flagged as shortage-related.
response.methods: Incident reports are searched with pre-specified product and concentration terms and matched to episode dates; the pharmacy intervention log is reviewed for the same products. A written definition of a substitution-related error is fixed before extraction, and a second pharmacist classifies a random 20 percent. Rates use doses dispensed as the denominator and are compared with the three months before each episode.
response.results: No data have been extracted; the privacy decision is pending.
response.discussion: No external evidence was retrieved in two recorded searches, so the discussion will describe local rates without comparison with other hospitals. It will focus on where in the medication process errors arose and what the next substitution plan should change.
response.limitations: Under-reporting in incident reports; one hospital; small numbers per episode.
response.conclusion: To be written. Results will be reported by episode, never by staff member or ward.
response.reportingChecklist: RECORD (STROBE extension for routinely collected data)
